catalog_quote: In all varieties of Fenghuang Xong, tone is primarily a syllable-level phenomenon. With only a few exceptions (see Section 3.6), each syllable produced in isolation in any variety of Fenghuang Xong will be accompanied by one of eight lexically specified tones. These “tones” are not simply specified pitch heights or contours; rather, they are each a complex “source list” consisting of a specified pitch height, a specified pitch contour, and a specified phonation type (e.g. modal, breathy, creaky). ... [p.9:] Xong appears to possess at least two distinct suprasegmental systems: a syllable-level system of lexically specified tones [...] and a phrase-level system of intonation contours overlaid on those tones (Section 3.6).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Xong is described as fully tonal: every syllable (bar a handful of toneless particles/interjections) carries one of eight lexical tone-phonation bundles; the only other suprasegmental system the author identifies is phrase-level intonation. No word-level stress or accent is described anywhere in the grammar; the notion is simply absent.
new_statements.exceptions: Toneless particles and interjections (sec. 3.6, 9.2.1, 11.3) whose pitch/duration vary with sentence modality; emphatic/focus 'exaggeration' of tones; utterance-final pitch fall. Separately, Ratliff 2010:199 (held) states family-wide that Hmong-Mien nominal prefixes 'are unstressed' (Jiwei Qo Xiong qo1- etc.), the only explicit stress remark found bearing on this language.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone = syllable/lexical level; intonation = polysyllabic phonological phrase/utterance level; monosyllables elicited in isolation are treated as full utterances subject to utterance-final fall. Variety: Yankan Village (La'ershan), Fenghuang County.
new_statements.identity_note: Sposato 2015 describes 'Fenghuang Xong', chiefly the variety of Yankan Village (La'ershan Town, Fenghuang County, W Hunan), with notes on Shanjiang and Zhuigaolai varieties; all fall under Western Xiangxi Miao [west2430 / ISO mmr] (the Jiwei standard, Huayuan County, is the same language; Sposato notes Jiwei has 6 tones vs 8 in Fenghuang and no reported toneless syllables). Ratliff 2010's statement is family-level (Hmong-Mien) with Jiwei 'Qo Xiong' examples, not a Xong-specific description.

sources.locator: Sec. 3.5.1 'Overview', p. 94 (PDF p. 109); with sec. 1.4 p. 9 (PDF p. 24) and sec. 3.6 p. 117 (PDF p. 132)
sources.note: Nothing: 'stress' never used phonologically in 674 pp. Ch.3: every syllable bears one of 8 lexical tones (sec.3.5.1 p.94) except a few toneless particles/interjections; sec.3.6 p.117 describes only a phrase-level intonation system (utterance-final fall, emphatic tone exaggeration, interrogative intonation); sec.1.4 p.9 'at least two distinct suprasegmental systems': syllable-level tone + phrase-level intonation. Nominal prefixes (ghaob- etc.) carry full tone -b and undergo regular sandhi; no reduction/stress remarks.
